Introduction

Skin appendages include hair follicles, sebaceous glands, sweat glands (eccrine & apocrine), and nails. Infections of these structures are common in clinical practice and range from superficial to deep, requiring different management.

1. Folliculitis

  • Definition — superficial inflammation of hair follicle; small (<5 mm) erythematous papules or pustules centred on hair follicle.
  • Causes — S. aureus (most common); Pseudomonas aeruginosa (hot tub folliculitis); Candida; Malassezia (Pityrosporum folliculitis); Molluscum contagiosum; herpes simplex; Gram-negative folliculitis (acne treatment).
  • Types — superficial (Bockhart's impetigo — S. aureus), deep, eosinophilic (Ofuji), Gram-negative, pityrosporum.
  • Clinical — itchy papules & pustules in hair-bearing areas (beard, scalp, axilla, buttocks, thighs).
  • Treatment — topical mupirocin, clindamycin, benzoyl peroxide; oral antibiotics for extensive (dicloxacillin, cephalexin); warm compresses.

2. Furuncle (Boil)

  • Definition — deep infection of hair follicle extending into subcutaneous tissue; painful, erythematous, fluctuant nodule with central necrotic plug (pustule).
  • Cause — S. aureus (>90%); MRSA increasing.
  • Sites — neck, face, axilla, buttocks, thighs, breast; often in adolescents & young adults.
  • Clinical — painful nodule enlarging over days; central yellow pustule ruptures, discharging pus & necrotic core; regional lymphadenitis.
  • Treatment — warm compresses (encourage spontaneous drainage); incision & drainage (I&D); dicloxacillin/cephalexin if surrounding cellulitis, fever, immunocompromised, or facial lesion.

3. Carbuncle

  • Definition — coalescence of multiple furuncles involving adjacent follicles, with drainage through multiple openings on skin surface.
  • Cause — S. aureus (including MRSA).
  • Sites — back of neck, shoulders, thighs, buttocks (thick skin); rare in face.
  • Clinical — larger, more painful than furuncle; systemic symptoms (fever, malaise); multiple draining sinuses; slower healing; scar formation.
  • Risk factors — diabetes, malnutrition, immunocompromise, obesity, poor hygiene.
  • Treatment — I&D + antibiotics (dicloxacillin/cephalexin; vancomycin if MRSA); control diabetes; treat carriers.

4. Hidradenitis Suppurativa (Acne Inversa)

  • Definition — chronic, recurrent, deep inflammation of apocrine sweat glands; painful nodules, abscesses, sinus tracts, scarring.
  • Sites — axillae, groin, buttocks, inframammary folds, perianal.
  • Cause — follicular occlusion → secondary bacterial infection (S. aureus, anaerobes, Streptococcus, Gram-negative bacilli); genetic predisposition.
  • Clinical — Hurley stages I (single/multiple abscesses, no sinus tracts/scars), II (recurrent abscesses with sinus tracts & scarring, single or multiple widely separated lesions), III (diffuse involvement with multiple interconnected tracts & abscesses).
  • Treatment — topical clindamycin; oral tetracycline/clindamycin + rifampin; adalimumab (anti-TNF — first FDA-approved biologic); surgery (wide local excision); lifestyle (weight loss, smoking cessation).

5. Sweat Gland Infections

  • Miliaria (heat rash / prickly heat)
    • Occlusion of eccrine sweat ducts; retention of sweat.
    • Types — Miliaria crystallina (superficial vesicles), Miliaria rubra (erythematous papules — "prickly heat"), Miliaria profunda (flesh-coloured papules — chronic).
    • Treatment — cooling, dry environment, calamine; secondary bacterial infection may require antibiotics.
  • Apocrine gland infection (hidradenitis suppurativa) — as above.

6. Nail & Nail Fold Infections

  • Paronychia
    • Infection of nail fold (proximal/lateral).
    • Acute — S. aureus (most common); painful, erythematous, fluctuant swelling; treatment — warm soaks, I&D if abscess, oral antibiotics (dicloxacillin).
    • Chronic — Candida albicans; dishwashers, bartenders, diabetics; boggy nail fold, nail dystrophy; treatment — topical antifungal (miconazole, clotrimazole), keep dry, oral itraconazole for refractory.
  • Felon
    • Deep infection of distal finger pulp.
    • Cause — S. aureus; puncture wound.
    • Clinical — severe throbbing pain, swelling, tense pulp; risk of necrosis & osteomyelitis.
    • Treatment — urgent I&D (lateral incision), oral antibiotics.
  • Onychomycosis (tinea unguium)
    • Fungal infection of nail plate.
    • Causes — Trichophyton rubrum (most common), T. mentagrophytes, Epidermophyton floccosum; Candida; non-dermatophyte moulds (Scopulariopsis, Aspergillus).
    • Types — distal subungual (most common), proximal subungual (HIV), white superficial, candidal, total dystrophic.
    • Treatment — oral terbinafine 250 mg OD × 6 weeks (fingernails) / 12 weeks (toenails); itraconazole pulse; topical efinaconazole, tavaborole for mild.
  • Herpetic whitlow
    • HSV-1 or HSV-2 infection of finger; painful vesicles; healthcare workers, children with oral HSV.
    • Treatment — oral acyclovir/valacyclovir; do NOT incise (delayed healing, secondary infection).

7. Hair & Sebaceous Gland Infections

  • Acne vulgaris
    • Disorder of pilosebaceous unit — increased sebum, keratin plug, Cutibacterium acnes (formerly Propionibacterium acnes) colonisation, inflammation.
    • Comedones (open/closed), papules, pustules, nodules, cysts, scars.
    • Treatment — topical retinoids (adapalene, tretinoin), benzoyl peroxide, antibiotics (clindamycin), oral isotretinoin for severe.
  • Tinea capitis
    • Dermatophyte infection of hair shaft & scalp; Microsporum, Trichophyton.
    • Types — endothrix (within shaft — "black dot"), ectothrix (outside shaft), favus (crust + scutula).
    • Treatment — oral griseofulvin × 6–8 weeks; terbinafine, itraconazole; selenium sulphide shampoo.
  • Ringworm (tinea corporis, cruris, pedis)
    • Dermatophyte infection of keratinised skin; Trichophyton, Microsporum, Epidermophyton.
    • Treatment — topical clotrimazole, miconazole, terbinafine; oral for extensive/recurrent.

Clinical Pearl

The single most important clinical decision in skin appendage infections is whether or not to drain an abscess — antibiotics alone cannot penetrate the abscess wall. Furuncles <5 mm can often drain spontaneously with warm compresses; larger lesions require I&D. Always suspect MRSA in recurrent skin abscesses, especially if there is a household contact with similar lesions, recent antibiotic use, hospitalisation, or sports team involvement. Send pus for culture & sensitivity — guide therapy. For recurrent furunculosis, address predisposing factors — diabetes, nasal carriage of S. aureus (decolonise with mupirocin), immunodeficiency, hygiene, nutrition. Herpetic whitlow must NOT be incised — it is viral, not bacterial, and I&D causes delayed healing & superinfection. Acne is not an infection — it is a disorder of the pilosebaceous unit; antibiotics are used for their anti-inflammatory effect, not antimicrobial — hence the rise of C. acnes antibiotic resistance and the move toward non-antibiotic therapies (benzoyl peroxide, retinoids, isotretinoin).

(A) Clinical Diagnosis (1 mark)

The clinical picture — 7-year-old unimmunised child with high-grade fever, toxicity, severe sore throat, inability to swallow, and white patch on the fauces that bleeds when touched — is the classic presentation of pharyngeal diphtheria.

(B) Etiological Agent (1 mark)

Corynebacterium diphtheriae — a Gram-positive, non-spore-forming, non-motile, non-capsulated pleomorphic bacillus. Characteristic morphology — Chinese letter / cuneiform (club-shaped) arrangement; metachromatic granules (volutin granules) on Loeffler's methylene blue or Albert stain. The club shape is due to presence of polyphosphate granules at poles.

Biotypes (based on colony morphology & haemolysis on tellurite blood agar):

  • gravis — large, grey, daisy-head colonies; most severe; associated with epidemics.
  • intermedius — small, flat, black colonies; intermediate severity.
  • mitis — small, glossy, black colonies; mildest; common in endemic areas.
  • belfanti — non-lipophilic variant.

Toxigenic strains carry the tox gene (encoded by corynephage β — a lysogenic bacteriophage); non-toxigenic strains cause mild pharyngitis but not classic diphtheria. Only toxigenic strains produce diphtheria toxin.

(C) Pathogenesis (5 marks)

1. Source & Transmission

  • Source — cases (symptomatic) & asymptomatic carriers (nasopharyngeal colonisation).
  • Transmission — droplet (coughing, sneezing); direct contact with wound exudate (cutaneous diphtheria); fomites (rare).
  • Incubation — 2–5 days (range 1–10 days).
  • Risk factors — unimmunised or incompletely immunised child; overcrowding; poor nutrition; immunocompromise; travel to endemic area.

2. Colonisation & Pseudomembrane Formation

  1. Adherence — via pili & surface proteins (DIP0733, DIP1281); C. diphtheriae colonises mucosa of tonsils, pharynx, larynx, nose; occasionally conjunctiva, genital mucosa, or skin (cutaneous diphtheria in tropics).
  2. Local invasion — bacteria remain superficial; do NOT invade deeper tissues or bloodstream.
  3. Pseudomembrane formation — bacteria + necrotic epithelial cells + fibrin + neutrophils + RBCs form a tough, adherent, grey-white membrane. Bleeds on attempted removal — characteristic. Extends from tonsils → uvula → soft palate → pharynx → larynx → trachea (causing airway obstruction).
  4. "Bull neck" — marked cervical lymphadenopathy with subcutaneous oedema; severe case sign.

3. Diphtheria Toxin — Mode of Action

  • Structure — AB toxin; 62 kDa single polypeptide.
    • A subunit (Fragment A, 21 kDa) — active catalytic moiety; released by proteolytic cleavage of disulfide bond.
    • B subunit (Fragment B, 41 kDa) — binding & translocation; binds heparin-binding epidermal growth factor-like (HB-EGF) receptor on host cells.
  • Cell entry
    1. B subunit binds HB-EGF receptor (all nucleated cells express; heart, nerves, kidneys particularly sensitive).
    2. Receptor-mediated endocytosis → endosome.
    3. Acidification of endosome triggers conformational change → B subunit forms pore in endosomal membrane.
    4. A subunit translocates through pore into cytoplasm.
    5. Disulfide bond reduced → A subunit released.
  • Enzymatic action
    • A subunit catalyses ADP-ribosylation of Elongation Factor 2 (EF-2) at diphthamide residue (unique modified histidine).
    • Uses NAD⁺ as cofactor → transfers ADP-ribose to diphthamide.
    • Modified EF-2 cannot bind ribosome → protein synthesis inhibited → cell death.
  • Toxin gene regulation
    • tox gene encoded by corynephage β (lysogenic phage); only toxigenic strains produce toxin.
    • DtxR (diphtheria toxin repressor) — iron-dependent regulatory protein.
      • High iron (Fe²⁺) → DtxR-Fe²⁺ binds tox operator → represses toxin gene.
      • Low iron → DtxR releases → toxin gene transcribed → toxin produced.
    • Explains why diphtheria is worse in iron-deficient hosts (low iron → high toxin).

4. Clinical Effects of Toxin

  • Local — necrotic pharyngitis; pseudomembrane; airway obstruction (laryngeal diphtheria — "membranous croup"); cervical adenitis with oedema ("bull neck").
  • Myocarditis — occurs 1–2 weeks after onset; ECG changes (ST-T changes, arrhythmias, heart block); cardiogenic shock; most common cause of death.
  • Neuropathy
    • Palatal paralysis (early — 2–3 weeks) — nasal regurgitation, nasal voice.
    • Oculomotor, facial, pharyngeal paralysis (3–5 weeks).
    • Polyneuropathy (paralytic syndrome) — symmetric, descending; resembles Guillain-Barré; occurs 1–3 months after onset.
  • Renal — acute tubular necrosis.
  • Adrenal — haemorrhage & insufficiency.

(D) Laboratory Diagnosis (5 marks)

1. Specimen

  • Throat swab / nasopharyngeal swab — collect from edge of pseudomembrane (not centre — necrotic); use dacron or rayon swab (not cotton — inhibits growth); avoid touching tongue/oropharynx.
  • Transport — immediate plating; if delay, use Amies or Stuart's transport medium with charcoal; refrigerate.
  • Cutaneous diphtheria — swab from wound edge.

2. Direct Microscopy (Gram & Albert Stain)

  • Gram stain — Gram-positive bacilli, pleomorphic (club-shaped, V, L, Y, Chinese letter arrangement); no spores, no capsules.
  • Albert's stain (or Loeffler's methylene blue) — metachromatic (volutin) granules appear black/dark purple against green/blue cytoplasm; pathognomonic for C. diphtheriae (also seen in C. pseudotuberculosis, C. xerosis; not 100% specific).
  • Limitation — microscopy alone cannot distinguish toxigenic from non-toxigenic strains; cannot exclude diphtheria.

3. Culture

Medium Colony appearance
Loeffler's serum slopeSmall, white, glistening colonies; rapid growth (6–8 h); enhances granule formation
Tinsdale medium (tellurite blood agar)Black colonies with brown halo (halo due to cystinase activity); selective for C. diphtheriae; differentiates biotypes (gravis = daisy-head; intermedius = small flat; mitis = small glossy)
Blood tellurite agar (BTA)Black or grey colonies; selective (potassium tellurite inhibits other flora); tells apart biotypes
Hoyle's tellurite agarSimilar to BTA; rapid (18 h)
McLeod's agarSelective; biotype differentiation
Blood agarSmall, white, haemolytic (mitis — β-haemolytic) colonies; non-selective (overgrown by normal flora)

4. Identification

  • Gram stain — typical Chinese letter arrangement.
  • Albert stain — metachromatic granules.
  • Biochemical tests
    • Catalase — positive.
    • Oxidase — negative.
    • Cystinase — positive (brown halo on Tinsdale).
    • Pyrzinamidase — negative (distinguishes from non-pathogenic corynebacteria).
    • Nitrate reduction — positive (most strains; gravis, mitis); intermedius may be negative.
    • Sugar fermentation — glucose +, maltose +, sucrose – (except mitis — variable); distinguishes from diphtheroids.
    • Urease — negative.
  • Elek test (gel precipitation) — gold standard for toxigenicity testing.
    • Filter paper strip soaked with diphtheria antitoxin embedded in agar plate.
    • Test strain streaked perpendicular to strip; non-toxigenic control also streaked.
    • Incubate 24–48 h; toxin diffuses from strain, antitoxin diffuses from strip → precipitation lines at 45° angle.
    • Precipitin lines from test strain joining those of positive control = toxigenic strain.
  • PCR for tox gene — rapid (4 h); detects tox gene; differentiates toxigenic from non-toxigenic strains.
  • Immunochromatographic test (ICT) — rapid bedside test for toxin detection.
  • Tissue culture test — observe cytopathic effect on HeLa or Vero cells; neutralisation by specific antitoxin confirms toxin.
  • MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry — rapid identification (minutes).

5. Other Tests

  • Complete blood count — leucocytosis; thrombocytopenia.
  • ECG — ST-T changes, arrhythmias, heart block (myocarditis).
  • Echocardiography — decreased ejection fraction.
  • Cardiac enzymes (troponin) — elevated.
  • Renal function — may be impaired.
  • Schick test — historical intradermal test for susceptibility (toxin + antitoxin); now obsolete.

(E) Prophylaxis (3 marks)

1. Active Immunisation — Diphtheria Toxoid Vaccine

  • Toxoid — formaldehyde-treated diphtheria toxin; loses toxicity but retains antigenicity; adsorbed on aluminium hydroxide adjuvant.
  • Types
    • DTP — diphtheria toxoid (D — 25 Lf) + tetanus toxoid + whole-cell pertussis.
    • DTaP — diphtheria toxoid + tetanus toxoid + acellular pertussis.
    • Tdap / Td — reduced dose diphtheria toxoid (2 Lf) + tetanus + acellular pertussis (booster for adolescents & adults).
    • Pentavalent vaccine — DTP + Hepatitis B + Hib (used in India's UIP).
  • Schedule (India — NIS)
    • 3 primary doses at 6, 10, 14 weeks.
    • 2 boosters at 16–18 months & 5 years.
    • Then Td at 10 & 16 years.
  • Efficacy — >95% after complete primary series; wanes over 10 years → boosters needed.
  • Adult boosters — Td every 10 years (often missed in adults).

2. Post-Exposure Prophylaxis (PEP) for Contacts

  • Identify close contacts — household, school, daycare; clinical & microbiological surveillance for 7 days.
  • Immunisation status
    • <3 doses or unknown — start primary series + booster.
    • ≥3 doses, last >5 years ago — booster dose.
    • Fully immunised, recent booster — no vaccine.
  • Antibiotic prophylaxis
    • Benzathine penicillin G 600,000–1,200,000 U IM single dose (children <30 kg → 600,000; ≥30 kg → 1,200,000).
    • Or azithromycin 500 mg OD × 5 days (children 10 mg/kg) — alternative if penicillin allergy.
    • Or erythromycin 500 mg QID × 7 days.
    • Or clindamycin.
  • Cultures — baseline & post-prophylaxis to confirm clearance.

3. Treatment of Cases

  • Diphtheria antitoxin (DAT) — equine-derived; given IV/IM ASAP (do NOT wait for culture confirmation if clinical suspicion high).
    • Dose — 20,000–40,000 U for pharyngeal/laryngeal disease <48 h; 80,000–120,000 U for extensive disease >48 h or neck swelling.
    • Always test for hypersensitivity (skin test or slow IV test dose) — risk of anaphylaxis or serum sickness.
    • Neutralises circulating toxin only — does NOT reverse tissue-bound toxin; therefore must be given early.
  • Antibiotics
    • IV Penicillin G (or procaine penicillin) × 14 days; or erythromycin × 14 days (penicillin allergy).
    • Eliminates organism, stops toxin production, prevents transmission.
    • Does NOT neutralise existing toxin — must be combined with antitoxin.
  • Supportive
    • Airway management — tracheostomy if laryngeal obstruction.
    • Bed rest (2–3 weeks) — minimises cardiac stress.
    • Cardiac monitoring — ECG, echocardiography; treat arrhythmias, heart failure.
    • Aspiration precautions for palatal paralysis; NG tube feeding.
    • ICU support if severe.
  • Isolation — droplet precautions until 2 negative cultures (24 h apart) after antibiotics completed.

Clinical Pearl

Diphtheria is a re-emerging infection in India — outbreaks reported in Kerala, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Assam, Delhi in last decade; largely due to waning immunity in adults (booster doses missed) & pockets of unimmunised children. The pseudomembrane that bleeds on touching is pathognomonic — but do NOT attempt to remove it (causes bleeding, aspiration, sudden airway obstruction). Always give diphtheria antitoxin (DAT) immediately on clinical suspicion — do NOT wait for culture confirmation — because antitoxin neutralises only free (unbound) toxin; once toxin binds to tissues, it cannot be reversed. Mortality is 5–10% even with treatment; respiratory obstruction or myocarditis are the main causes of death. The Schick test (intradermal toxin injection) is historical — replaced by serology; an antitoxin level >0.1 IU/mL is considered protective. The most important prevention is complete childhood immunisation + adult Td boosters every 10 years. All healthcare workers should have current Tdap vaccination. The recent shift from DTP to DTaP in many countries (less reactogenic) has reduced adverse events but may reduce durability — acellular pertussis immunity wanes faster.
q1_1_3_25:
Introduction

Aspergillosis refers to a spectrum of diseases caused by moulds of the genus Aspergillus, most commonly Aspergillus fumigatus (~80% of human infections); also A. flavus, A. niger, A. terreus, A. nidulans. Aspergillus is ubiquitous in environment — soil, decaying vegetation, compost, dust, air conditioning systems. Inhalation of conidia (spores) is the primary route of infection.

Clinical Syndromes

1. Allergic Bronchopulmonary Aspergillosis (ABPA)

  • Hypersensitivity reaction to Aspergillus antigens in patients with asthma or cystic fibrosis.
  • Recurrent wheeze, cough, brownish sputum plugs (mucus plugs containing hyphae), fleeting pulmonary infiltrates, eosinophilia.
  • Pathogenesis — IgE-mediated Type I + immune complex Type III hypersensitivity.
  • Diagnosis — Rosenberg-Patterson criteria (asthma, immediate skin reactivity to Aspergillus, total IgE >1000 IU/mL, elevated Aspergillus-specific IgE/IgG, eosinophilia, pulmonary infiltrates, central bronchiectasis).
  • Treatment — oral corticosteroids (prednisolone); itraconazole (antifungal — reduces steroid requirement); omalizumab (anti-IgE) in refractory.

2. Aspergilloma (Fungus Ball / Mycetoma)

  • Colonisation of pre-existing pulmonary cavity (TB, sarcoid, bronchiectasis) by Aspergillus; forms a ball of fungal hyphae mixed with mucus & cellular debris.
  • Often asymptomatic; may cause haemoptysis (sometimes massive & life-threatening — erosion into adjacent bronchial artery); chronic cough.
  • Imaging — chest X-ray / CT: round/oval mass with crescent of air ("air crescent" sign / Monod's sign) within a cavity, typically in upper lobe; gravity-dependent movement on changing position.
  • Serology — Aspergillus precipitating antibody (IgG) positive.
  • Treatment — surgical resection (lobectomy) for significant haemoptysis; antifungals have poor penetration into cavity; bronchial artery embolisation for acute bleeding.

3. Chronic Pulmonary Aspergillosis (CPA / Chronic Necrotising Pulmonary Aspergillosis)

  • Slowly progressive infection in patients with underlying lung disease (COPD, old TB, sarcoidosis) but mild immunocompromise.
  • Subacute course — weeks to months; cough, weight loss, haemoptysis, fever.
  • Imaging — progressive cavity with surrounding infiltrate; pleural thickening.
  • Diagnosis — culture/histology from biopsy; Aspergillus IgG positive; galactomannan may be positive.
  • Treatment — long-term oral itraconazole or voriconazole (≥6 months); surgical resection if localised.

4. Invasive Pulmonary Aspergillosis (IPA) — Most Severe

  • Occurs in severely immunocompromised — neutropenia (<500/µL), haematological malignancy (AML, ALL), stem cell transplant, solid organ transplant, prolonged high-dose steroids, advanced HIV.
  • Angioinvasive — hyphae invade blood vessels → thrombosis, infarction, haemorrhagic necrosis; disseminates haematogenously to brain, heart, kidney, liver, skin, GI.
  • Clinical — fever (often refractory to broad-spectrum antibiotics), pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis, dyspnoea, cough; may mimic pulmonary embolism.
  • Imaging — CT chest: halo sign (nodular lesion surrounded by ground-glass opacity — haemorrhage); later air crescent sign (cavitation as neutrophils recover); multiple nodules.
  • Diagnosis — galactomannan antigen (serum, BAL); PCR; culture; histopathology (biopsy).
  • Treatment — voriconazole IV/PO (drug of choice; reduces mortality vs amphotericin); isavuconazole; amphotericin B lipid formulation; caspofungin ( salvage); echinocandin. Reverse immunosuppression if possible.
  • Mortality 40–60% even with treatment; >90% untreated.

5. Invasive Sinus Aspergillosis

  • Acute invasive — in immunocompromised; similar to mucormycosis; rapidly progressive; angioinvasive; orbital cellulitis, cranial nerve palsy, cerebral extension.
  • Chronic invasive — in immunocompetent / diabetic; slowly progressive sinus disease; bony erosion.
  • Aspergillus granuloma (paranasal sinus fungus ball) — non-invasive mass of hyphae in sinus; chronic sinusitis; surgical removal.
  • Treatment — surgical debridement + antifungal (voriconazole).

6. Disseminated Aspergillosis

  • Haematogenous spread from lung; brain (cerebral aspergillosis — ring-enhancing lesions, stroke, abscess); heart (endocarditis); skin (multiple papules, nodules, eschars); kidney; liver; GI.
  • Often fatal.

7. Other Forms

  • Aspergillus endocarditis — prosthetic valve; culture-negative; large friable vegetations; emboli.
  • Cerebral aspergillosis — ring-enhancing lesion; haemorrhagic infarct; abscess; high mortality.
  • Cutaneous aspergillosis — primary (traumatic inoculation); secondary (disseminated); necrotising skin lesions.
  • Otomycosis — Aspergillus (especially A. niger — black tufts) in external auditory canal; pruritus, discharge; topical antifungal.
  • Keratitis — corneal infection; trauma, contact lens; Aspergillus; topical natamycin, amphotericin.
  • Onychomycosis — nail infection; A. niger.
  • Gastrointestinal aspergillosis — rare; in neutropenia; ulceration, bleeding, perforation.

Pathogenesis

  • Conidia (spores) inhaled; small size (2–3 µm) allows reach alveoli.
  • Adhesion — conidia adhere to epithelial cells & extracellular matrix (laminin, fibrinogen).
  • Germination — conidia germinate into hyphae at 37 °C; hyphae invade tissue.
  • Angioinvasion — hyphae invade blood vessels (especially in immunocompromised); thrombosis, infarction, haematogenous dissemination.
  • Virulence factors:
    • Galactomannan — cell wall polysaccharide; released during growth; diagnostic marker.
    • β-1,3-glucan — cell wall component.
    • Pigments (melanin, gliotoxin) — antioxidant; immune evasion; cytotoxic (apoptosis of immune cells).
    • Proteases, elastases, phospholipases — tissue invasion.
    • Siderophores — iron acquisition.
    • Aflatoxin (A. flavus) — carcinogen; not directly related to aspergillosis.
  • Host defences — macrophages (ingest conidia); neutrophils (kill hyphae via oxidative burst, NETs); T cells (Th1, Th17).

Laboratory Diagnosis

1. Specimen

  • Sputum, BAL (bronchoalveolar lavage), tracheal aspirate.
  • Blood — serum for galactomannan, β-D-glucan; PCR; (blood culture usually negative — angioinvasive but does not septate in blood).
  • Tissue biopsy — lung, sinus, brain, skin.
  • CSF — for cerebral aspergillosis (galactomannan, PCR; culture usually negative).
  • Ear swab — otomycosis.
  • Corneal scrape — keratitis.

2. Direct Microscopy

  • KOH mount / Calcofluor white — septate hyphae, acute-angle (45°) branching; 3–6 µm wide; characteristic of Aspergillus (also seen in other hyaline moulds — Fusarium, Scedosporium — cannot distinguish).
  • Contrast with Mucorales — broad (6–15 µm), ribbon-like, aseptate (pauciseptate), right-angle (90°) branching.
  • Gram stain — may show hyphae.
  • Histopathology — septate acute-angle hyphae invading tissue; GMS (Grocott methenamine silver) or PAS stain; angioinvasion; necrosis.

3. Culture

  • Sabouraud dextrose agar (SDA) — without cycloheximide (inhibits Aspergillus); incubate at 25–30 °C for 3–7 days.
  • Blood agar, potato dextrose agar, Czapek-Dox agar.
  • Colony morphology:
    • A. fumigatus — smoky green to grey-green colonies; velvety or powdery; reverse white to tan.
    • A. flavus — yellow-green (olive); also produces aflatoxin.
    • A. niger — black colonies (carbon black); white reverse; common in otomycosis.
    • A. terreus — cinnamon-brown; amphotericin B resistant.
    • A. nidulans — green to buff.

4. Microscopic Identification

  • Lactophenol cotton blue mount — reveals conidiophore structure:
    • Foot cell — basal hyphal cell from which conidiophore arises.
    • Conidiophore (vesicle) — swollen at tip.
    • Phialides — bottle-shaped cells; may cover entire vesicle (A. fumigatus — uniseriate, upper half only) or be in two rows (biseriate — A. flavus, A. niger).
    • Conidia — chains of small round spores; cover vesicle ("spore head").
  • A. fumigatus — uniseriate; phialides on upper half of vesicle; columnar spore chains.
  • A. niger — biseriate; phialides cover entire vesicle; large globular head; black conidia.
  • A. flavus — biseriate; phialides cover entire vesicle; yellow-green conidia.

5. Antigen Detection

  • Galactomannan (GM) antigen:
    • Aspergillus cell wall polysaccharide; released during growth.
    • Serum — sensitivity 70–85%, specificity 90–95%; 2 samples/week in high-risk patients.
    • BAL — higher sensitivity (80–90%); cut-off index ≥0.5 (serum) or ≥1.0 (BAL).
    • CSF — for cerebral aspergillosis.
    • False positive — piperacillin-tazobactam, amoxicillin-clavulanate (historical — formulations now improved); cross-reactivity with other moulds (Penicillium, Fusarium, Histoplasma); Gluconobacter bacteraemia; neonates; double-fraction wheat.
    • False negative — antifungal prophylaxis (reduces fungal load).
  • β-D-glucan:
    • Cell wall component shared with Candida, Fusarium, Pneumocystis — NOT specific for Aspergillus.
    • Useful screening for invasive fungal infection; 2 serial positives.
    • False positive — haemodialysis, IVIG, albumin, gauze.

6. Molecular Tests

  • PCR — Aspergillus DNA in blood, BAL, CSF, tissue; targets 18S rRNA, 28S rRNA, ITS region; sensitivity & specificity vary.
  • Real-time PCR — quantitative; faster.
  • Combined galactomannan + PCR improves diagnostic accuracy.

7. Other Tests

  • Skin test — Aspergillus antigen; immediate hypersensitivity (Type I) for ABPA diagnosis.
  • Serology:
    • Total IgE — elevated in ABPA (>1000 IU/mL).
    • Aspergillus-specific IgE — ABPA.
    • Aspergillus precipitating antibody (IgG) — aspergilloma, CPA; positive in 90%.
    • Aspergillus-specific IgG ELISA — chronic pulmonary aspergillosis.
  • Imaging:
    • Chest CT — halo sign (early); air crescent sign (late); nodules; consolidation; cavitation.
    • Chest X-ray — non-specific.
    • Sinus CT — bony erosion, sinus opacity.
    • Brain MRI — ring-enhancing lesions; haemorrhagic infarct.
  • Bronchoscopy — BAL for microscopy, culture, galactomannan, PCR; transbronchial biopsy for histopathology.

EORTC/MSG Diagnostic Criteria for Invasive Aspergillosis

Definite — histopathology + culture from sterile site. Probable — host factor + clinical feature + mycological evidence. Possible — host factor + clinical feature alone.

Prevention

  • Prophylaxis in high-risk patients (neutropenia, transplant) — posaconazole, itraconazole, voriconazole; aerosolised amphotericin B.
  • Protected environments — HEPA-filtered rooms; positive pressure; avoid plants/flowers.
  • Avoid dust exposure — construction sites; gardening (mask if gardening).
  • Reverse immunosuppression — reduce steroids; G-CSF for neutropenia.
  • Surveillance — galactomannan twice weekly in high-risk.

Clinical Pearl

The halo sign on CT chest (nodule surrounded by ground-glass opacity) in a neutropenic patient is highly suggestive of invasive pulmonary aspergillosis — start voriconazole empirically while awaiting confirmation. The air crescent sign (crescent of air around a nodular lesion) develops later — indicates cavitation as neutrophils recover & infarcted tissue separates from viable lung; heralds neutrophil recovery. Galactomannan antigen (serum & BAL) is the key non-culture diagnostic test — sensitivity 70–85% in serum, 80–90% in BAL; positive in serum of high-risk patient = probable invasive aspergillosis. Voriconazole is the drug of choice for invasive aspergillosis — superior to amphotericin B (Herbrecht et al. 2002 NEJM trial — improved survival). Always reverse immunosuppression — reduce steroids, G-CSF for neutropenia; without immune recovery, antifungals alone often fail. Aspergilloma (fungus ball) — surgical resection is definitive treatment for symptomatic haemoptysis; antifungals do NOT penetrate cavity well. ABPA — long-term steroids + itraconazole; check total IgE every 6–8 weeks (should fall with treatment); aim for IgE <2× baseline. A. terreus is resistant to amphotericin B — use voriconazole. Distinguish from Mucorales (mucormycosis) — Mucorales have broad aseptate right-angle branching hyphae, angioinvasive, rapidly progressive, poor response to voriconazole (drug of choice is liposomal amphotericin B + surgical debridement). COVID-associated pulmonary aspergillosis (CAPA) — emerging complication of severe COVID-19 (especially ICU patients on steroids); high mortality; galactomannan + BAL culture for diagnosis.
